To befriend someone means to deliberately act as a friend toward them — to reach out, show kindness, and build a friendly connection with them, especially when they need it.

It is an active word. You make the move. You take the step toward someone and treat them warmly, support them, or include them. The other person receives your friendship.

Think of it this way: if two people happen to become friends naturally over time, you might say they "became friends." But when you befriend someone, there is a conscious decision on your part — you choose to extend friendship to them.

"Befriend" carries a warm, generous tone. It quietly suggests that you are doing something kind — often for someone who is lonely, new, struggling, or in need of connection. It is not a cold or neutral word. When you befriend someone, you are essentially opening a door to them and saying, "You are welcome here."

• The subject (the person doing the action): the one who reaches out and offers friendship.
  • The object (the person receiving the action): the one who is befriended — often someone on the outside, someone alone, or someone unfamiliar.

She befriended the new girl in class.

Here, "she" is the one making the effort. The new girl is the one being welcomed.

You cannot accidentally befriend someone. The word always implies a purposeful act of kindness or connection. There is thought, warmth, and effort behind it.

This is what separates "befriending" from simply "meeting" someone or "getting along" with them.
The Word Works in Many Situations

Befriending is not only about humans. You can befriend:

  • A person — a classmate, a stranger, a neighbor, a colleague.
  • An animal — a stray dog, a shy cat, a wild bird you feed regularly.
  • A group — you can befriend an entire community of people.

Over the weeks, he befriended the stray cat that visited his porch every evening.

The volunteer befriended elderly residents at the care home who rarely had visitors.
Shades of Meaning — When It Goes Deeper

Sometimes "befriend" goes beyond just being friendly. It can suggest:

  1. Protection or support — befriending someone who is being bullied or excluded.
  2. Mentorship or guidance — a senior person befriending a younger, less experienced one.
  3. Emotional rescue — being there for someone going through a hard time.

In all these cases, the person doing the befriending is giving something — their time, care, attention, or loyalty.
How Formal or Informal Is It?

"Befriend" sits comfortably in both formal writing and everyday conversation, though it leans slightly toward formal or literary use. In casual speech, people might instead say "made friends with" or "got close to." But in writing — essays, stories, articles — "befriend" is natural, clean, and precise.
How to Use It in a Sentence

Here are several examples showing the word in different real-life situations:

  • "The teacher took the time to befriend her most withdrawn student."
  • "He was new to the city and found it hard to befriend anyone at first."
  • "She befriended a fellow traveler on the train, and they kept in touch for years."
  • "The charity's goal is to befriend isolated people in the community."
  • "It's not always easy to befriend someone who has been hurt before — they take time to trust."
To befriend someone = to take the initiative to become their friend, especially by showing kindness, warmth, or support to someone who needs it.

The power of this word is in its direction. It flows from you outward toward another person. It is a verb of generosity. When you befriend someone, you are choosing to make their world a little less lonely — and that is precisely why the word carries such quiet dignity.
